item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'll own up.

Gut: Did I enjoy it? 0 & 1s means I didn't like it, 2s meant I was neutral, and 3 and 4s meant I liked it. Fairly simple.

Originality: Did I think the article was unique? This applies not just to the format and approach to reimagining it (as well as the actual reimagining), but as well as the actual content itself and the ideas it had. Did it take a unique and interesting concept/idea? Or was it something cliched or something you see a lot in other media, but with something reimagined to fit it?

Execution: Were all the ideas and concepts done in a way that succeeded and could do what the author intended to do? Formatting plays a big role in this. While I could theoretically enjoy a story, if something was formatted in a way that was hard to get behind, I wouldn't rank it as high. In that way, it's separate from Gut.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like cyberpunk. That said:

Overall
I first read the original if I hadn't already, or was a bit hazy on the particulars. Then I read the reimagined entry. I'll note that there were no 0s in my scoring.

Gut
What it says on the box. I read the entry and asked myself what my gut reaction was. My gut and I are old friends, so this wasn't the hardest category to score for. I'll note that my gut was very pleased with the entries, with scores starting at 2 for "I enjoyed this", 3 for "That was awesome" and 4 for "MY MIND! SHE IS BLOWN!"

Originality
I judged entries on departure from the original article, both on a practical and a more abstract level, and on the packaging (i.e. what format was used, how was it used, and did it help the reimagining? I gave out a few 1s here, lots of 2s and a few 3s. No 4s.

Execution
Finally, I looked at whether or not the author had succeeded in blending a reimagined concept with the format, and how well they'd succeeded. A good spread of 1s, 2s and 3s here.

Like Clef, I didn't feel the need to penalize anyone.

item.title: Re: WINNERS!
item.content:encoded:
I used a similar interpretation to Clef for Originality and Execution, but for Gut Feeling, I was much less rigorous about it. I didn't factor the original article into it, because that felt unfair to people who chose better articles to reimagine, and introduced a confounding factor beyond how much I liked the article.

One thing I sort of wished we had, although I haven't really looked into the implications of this, would be one or two extra points a judge could give to one entry we feel deserves to win.

Then again, I guess that's called an upvote.

EDIT: Metacommentary!

  • I suspect that the reason EFT had such a high community score is in part because it was the first entry posted.
  • Likewise, PHD was the last entry posted, and so had the least time to garner upvotes. Plus, the community's initial excitement for the contest may have worn off.
  • You should see if you could figure out how much of the variation in community scores can be explained by post order or by exactly when they were posted.
  • Data did give out a wide range of scores, but seemed sort of bimodal in his distribution.
  • Teal'c's grades have remarkably little variation.

item.title: Re: WINNERS!
item.content:encoded:
I won't say which judge I was, but I will copy-paste the text I sent to Troy explaining how I interpreted the rubric.

For "Gut," I was mostly judging the content in comparison to the SCP in question. Namely: given a choice between the original article and the version in the contest entry, would I prefer the new version? Two articles got full marks there. A "3" here meant that it was a tough choice. 2 or lower: I generally preferred the version we have here. This did mean that those writers who chose less well-regarded articles had an advantage here.

For "Originality," I was judging the content based on departures from established canon. Here, a couple of articles scored flat 0s for simply using the original content without changes. There were a lot of 1s too: these were generally entries that either didn't depart enough from the original, or where the link back to the original is completely incomprehensible. The "sweet spot," which is where the "4s" lie, is when I can see the influences of the original, but the concept was taken in a radical new direction that made me sit and go "huh."

As for "Execution" - a 2 was a well-written article or tale without technical errors. For a 3, I needed to see some originality and real creativity. 4s were reserved for articles that took radical risks and stuck the landing. I don't think I gave out any 0s for execution, and my 1s were resolved for articles that were written competently, but didn't engage me.

I didn't feel the need to -2 penalty anyone.

EDIT: I did a quick spreadsheet here Some interesting results:

  • K-9 was the most generous.
  • Harlan Band was the least generous.
  • Data gave out the broadest range of scores.
  • Most controversial entries among judges: KK, Ph9, VP, ITD
  • Least controversial entry among judges: GM, which people seemed to feel was about average.
  • Least controversial entry between judges and community: ITD
  • Most controversial entry between judges and community: JAD
  • The 'Favored of the Unwashed Masses' Award: EFT. The Judges gave this one a middle of the road rating, but it had by far the highest adjusted community score.
  • The 'Fancied by the Ivory Tower Elite' Award: The judges seemed to feel PHD was about average, but the community gave it low marks.
  • The 'We Are All In Agreement' Award: EH. Everyone seemed to agree it was about average.
  • The 'We Cannot See Eye To Eye' Award: Again, EFT had the biggest discrepancy between judges and community.

item.title: WINNERS!
item.content:encoded:
Alright. Due to the complexity of the judging system on this contest, you’ll need to check out all the stuff below to see how your story ranked. Yayyyyy.

Concerning the system: other people (who shall remain nameless) promised people that the judge ratings would be worth two-thirds of the final score for the system. Because of this, I've broken the judges into two groups (we had fourteen friggin' judges!) and adjusted the rating scores by scaling the highest possible rating to the equivalent of the maximum possible judge points (if you're desperate for the exact system, I can post it, but given the small amount of increase in these scores — since the maximum possible judge rating was 84 and the highest rating was 81 — very little changed). Decimal points were retained to ensure a clear winner in the event of a tie.

Judge names are anonymous as always. Any judges wishing to come forward may. I'll be posting comments from the various judges in a few days.
